## Q1
Given below are the two statements:

Statement I: Any retrieval request that is specified in the basic relational algebra can also be specified in relational calculus.

Statement II: Any retrieval request that is specified in the relational calculus can also be specified in basic relational algebra.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

## Q1 - Options
(A) Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
(B) Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
(C) Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
(D) Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q86

Codd's equivalence result establishes that relational algebra and relational calculus have the same expressive power, so any query expressible in one can also be expressed in the other. Statement I holds directly, since relational algebra is by construction always expressible in relational calculus.

Statement II holds for safe relational calculus expressions, which is the form relational calculus is restricted to in standard database theory precisely so that every calculus query corresponds to an equivalent algebra expression, and an unrestricted (unsafe) calculus expression is not considered a valid query in the first place. Under this standard restriction, both statements are true, which is why relational algebra and relational calculus are described as equivalent in expressive power. This equivalence claim depends on the safety restriction being assumed rather than stated explicitly here, so it is worth confirming which convention the source course uses before treating this as settled.

## Q2
Use the following schema of the academic institution relational database:

student (rollno, name, degree, year, sex, deptno, advisor)<br>
department (deptid, name, hod, phone)<br>
professor (empid, name, sex, startyear, deptno, phone)<br>
course (courseid, cname, credits, deptno)<br>
enrollment (rollno, courseid, sem, year, grade)<br>
teaching (empid, courseid, sem, year, classroom)<br>
prerequisite (precourseid, courseid)

deptno is a foreign key in the student, professor and course relations referring to deptid of department. advisor is a foreign key in student referring to empid of professor. hod is a foreign key in department referring to empid of professor. rollno is a foreign key in enrollment referring to rollno of student. courseid is a foreign key in enrollment and teaching referring to courseid of course. empid is a foreign key of teaching referring to empid of professor. precourseid and courseid are foreign keys in prerequisite referring to courseid of course.

Which of the following queries would retrieve the roll number and names of students who have enrolled for all the prerequisite courses of the course number 324?

## Q2 - Options
(A) Select s.rollno, s.name From student s, enrollment e Where e.rollno = s.rollno and e.courseid = ANY (select precourseid from prerequisite p where p.courseid = "324")
(B) Select s.rollno, s.name From student s, enrollment e Where e.rollno = s.rollno and e.courseid = ALL (select precourseid from prerequisite p where p.courseid = "324")
(C) Select s.rollno, s.name From student s Where NOT EXISTS (select \* from prerequisite p where p.courseid = "324" and NOT EXISTS (select \* from enrollment e where e.courseid = p.precourseid and e.rollno = s.rollno))
(D) Select s.rollno, s.name From student s Where EXISTS (select \* from prerequisite p where p.courseid = "324") and EXISTS (select \* from enrollment e where e.courseid = p.precourseid and e.rollno = s.rollno)

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q90

Finding students enrolled in every prerequisite of course 324 is a universal ('for all') condition, which in SQL is standardly expressed with the double-negation, NOT EXISTS wrapped around another NOT EXISTS, division pattern rather than with ANY or ALL.

- **A. uses = ANY** — this only requires a match with at least one prerequisite course, which finds students who took at least one prerequisite rather than every one of them.
- **B. uses = ALL** — a single enrollment row's courseid cannot simultaneously equal every value in a multi-row prerequisite list, so this comparison does not correctly express enrollment in every prerequisite.
- **C. correct.** The inner NOT EXISTS finds any prerequisite course of 324 that the student has not enrolled in, and the outer NOT EXISTS then requires that no such missing prerequisite exists, which is exactly the standard relational-division idiom for "enrolled in all prerequisites."
- **D. uses EXISTS and EXISTS** — this only requires that course 324 has some prerequisite and that the student has enrolled in some course matching an uncorrelated reference, which does not enforce enrollment in every prerequisite either.

Since C correctly implements the universal quantification needed here, it is the right query.

## Q3
Use the following schema of the academic institution relational database:

student (rollno, name, degree, year, sex, deptno, advisor)<br>
department (deptid, name, hod, phone)<br>
professor (empid, name, sex, startyear, deptno, phone)<br>
course (courseid, cname, credits, deptno)<br>
enrollment (rollno, courseid, sem, year, grade)<br>
teaching (empid, courseid, sem, year, classroom)<br>
prerequisite (precourseid, courseid)

advisor is a foreign key in student referring to empid of professor.

Given query: select s.rollno from student s where s.sex = ALL (select f.sex from professor f where f.empid = s.advisor)

Consider the following statements about the given query, which retrieves the set of all students whose gender is the same as the gender of their advisor:

S1. It has a correlated subquery<br>
S2. It has an uncorrelated subquery<br>
S3. If we replace ALL by ANY in the above query, its result will be different<br>
S4. If we replace ALL by ANY in the above query, its result will be same.

Identify all the statements that are TRUE:

## Q3 - Options
(A) S1 and S3 are true
(B) S1 and S4 are true
(C) S2 and S3 are true
(D) S2 and S4 are true

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q91

The subquery references s.advisor, a column from the outer query's table s, so it must be re-evaluated for every outer row, making it a correlated subquery. S1 is true and S2, which claims the opposite, is false.

Since empid is the key of professor, the subquery select f.sex from professor f where f.empid=s.advisor returns at most one row for any given student. When a subquery returns a single value, comparing with = ALL and = ANY reduce to the exact same equality test against that one value, so swapping ALL for ANY here does not change the result. S4 is true and S3, which claims the result would differ, is false.

Since S1 and S4 are the true statements, the correct option is S1 and S4 are true.

## Q4
Use the following schema of the academic institution relational database:

department (deptid, name, hod, phone)<br>
course (courseid, cname, credits, deptno)

deptno is a foreign key in course referring to deptid of department.

Which of the following queries would compute, for each department, the total credits of all the courses offered by the department?

## Q4 - Options
(A) select deptid, name, sum(credits) as totalcredits from department, course where deptid=deptno group by deptid, name;
(B) select deptid, name, count(credits) as totalcredits from department, course where deptid=deptno group by deptid, name;
(C) select deptid, name, sum(credits) as totalcredits from department, course where deptid=deptno
(D) select deptid, name, sum(credits) as totalcredits from department, course group by deptid, name having deptid=deptno;

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q92

Computing a per-department total requires first joining department to course on the matching key, then grouping by department, and summing credits within each group.

- **A. correct.** It joins department and course on deptid=deptno in the WHERE clause, then groups by deptid and name, and sums credits within each group, which is exactly the standard join-then-aggregate pattern.
- **B. uses count(credits)** — this counts how many courses each department offers rather than adding up their credit values, so it does not compute total credits.
- **C. has no GROUP BY at all** — mixing an aggregate function like sum with non-aggregated columns such as deptid and name, with no grouping clause, does not produce one correctly aggregated row per department.
- **D. moves the join condition into HAVING and drops the WHERE join** — without first joining department to course, grouping department and course together directly cross-joins every department with every course before any filtering, which does not correctly restrict courses to their own department.

Since only A performs the join before grouping and aggregating correctly, it is the right query.

## Q5
Use the following schema of the academic institution relational database:

department (deptid, name, hod, phone)<br>
course (courseid, cname, credits, deptno)

deptno is a foreign key in course referring to deptid of department.

Which of the following queries would retrieve the dept id and name of all the departments that are such that the total of the credits of all the offered courses by the department is strictly greater than 40?

## Q5 - Options
(A) select deptid, name, sum(credits) as totalcredits from department, course where totalcredits &gt; 40 group by deptid, name having deptid = deptno;
(B) select deptid, name, sum(credits) as totalcredits from department, course where deptid = deptno and totalcredits &gt; 40 group by deptid, name;
(C) select deptid, name, sum(credits) as totalcredits from department, course group by deptid, name having deptid = deptno and totalcredits &gt; 40;
(D) select deptid, name, sum(credits) as totalcredits from department, course where deptid = deptno group by deptid, name having totalcredits &gt; 40;

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q93

A computed aggregate alias like totalcredits does not exist yet when the WHERE clause is evaluated, since WHERE filters rows before grouping and aggregation happen, so it can only be referenced afterward, in HAVING.

- **A and B reference totalcredits inside WHERE** — at that point in query evaluation, sum(credits) has not been computed yet, so this is not a valid way to filter on the aggregated total.
- **C moves the join condition deptid=deptno into HAVING and has no WHERE at all** — without joining department to course first, the query cross-joins every department with every course, so the grouped sums are not correctly restricted to each department's own courses.
- **D. correct.** It performs the join in WHERE first (deptid=deptno), then groups by department, and only then filters the aggregated total in HAVING (totalcredits &gt; 40), which is exactly where a computed aggregate can legally be filtered.

Since only D places the join before grouping and the aggregate filter in HAVING, it is the right query.

## Q6
Use the following schema of the academic institution relational database:

student (rollno, name, degree, year, sex, deptno, advisor)<br>
course (courseid, cname, credits, deptno)<br>
enrollment (rollno, courseid, sem, year, grade)

Given query:

select s.rollno, s.name from student s where EXISTS (select c.courseid from course c where c.deptno=5 and<br>
EXISTS (select e.\* from enrollment e where e.courseid = c.courseid and e.rollno = s.rollno));

Which one of the following statements is correct with respect to the given query?

## Q6 - Options
(A) It retrieves the roll number and names of students who have not enrolled for all courses offered by department number 5.
(B) It retrieves the roll number and names of students who have enrolled for all courses offered by department number 5.
(C) It retrieves the roll number and names of students who have enrolled for at least one course offered by department number 5.
(D) It retrieves the roll number and names of students who are such that there exists at least one course offered by department number 5 which is not enrolled by the student.

## Q6 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q94

The outer EXISTS asks whether there is at least one course c in department 5 for which the inner EXISTS also holds, and the inner EXISTS asks whether the student has an enrollment matching that specific course.

A single EXISTS is an existential ('at least one') quantifier, not a universal ('for all') one, so this query only requires finding one department-5 course the student has enrolled in, not every one of them.

This matches retrieving students who have enrolled for at least one course offered by department number 5, not the stronger "enrolled in all" or "not enrolled in some" readings described in the other options.

## Q7
Identify the incorrect statement(s).

## Q7 - Options
(A) A candidate key is minimal set of one or more attributes that, taken collectively, allows us to uniquely identify any entity in the entity set.
(B) A candidate key for which no proper subset is also a candidate key is called a super key.
(C) A super key is a set of one or more attributes that, taken collectively, allows us to uniquely identify any entity in the entity set.
(D) A super key for which no proper subset is also a super key is called a candidate key.

## Q7 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q14

Check each statement against the standard definitions: a super key uniquely identifies an entity, and a candidate key is a minimal super key (one with no proper subset that is also a super key).

- **A. Candidate key is a minimal uniquely-identifying attribute set** — correct, this is the standard definition.
- **B. A candidate key with no proper-subset candidate key is called a super key** — incorrect. This statement swaps the definitions: minimality applied to a candidate key does not produce a super key, it just restates what a candidate key already is.
- **C. A super key uniquely identifies an entity** — correct, this is the standard definition.
- **D. A super key with no proper-subset super key is called a candidate key** — correct, this is exactly the minimality condition that defines a candidate key.

## Q9
Identify the correct operation which produces the given output based on two relations R1 and R2.

| Relation | Name | Class |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | a1 | 9 |
| R1 | b1 | 5 |
| R1 | c1 | 6 |
| R1 | d1 | 11 |
| R2 | b1 | 5 |
| R2 | f1 | 8 |
| Output | b1 | 5 |

Relations R1, R2 and the resulting output

## Q9 - Options
(A) R1 ∩ R2
(B) R1 − R2
(C) R1 − (R1 − R2)
(D) R1 ∪ R2

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** A, C
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q50

Compare the tuples in R1 and R2 against the output, because the operation is identified by which rows survive.

R1 contains (a1,9), (b1,5), (c1,6), (d1,11), and R2 contains (b1,5), (f1,8). The output contains only (b1,5), which is the single tuple that appears in both relations.

Keeping only the tuples common to both relations is exactly the intersection operation, R1 ∩ R2.

R1 − (R1 − R2) computes the same result by a different route: R1 − R2 removes every R1 tuple that is also in R2, leaving only R1's own tuples, and subtracting that from R1 a second time leaves exactly the tuples R1 shares with R2. So R1 − (R1 − R2) is set-theoretically identical to R1 ∩ R2, and both are accepted here.

## Q10
A trigger is

## Q10 - Options
(A) A statement that enables to start DBMS.
(B) A statement that is executed by the user when debugging an application program.
(C) A condition the system tests for the validity of the database user.
(D) A statement that is executed automatically by the system as a side effect of modification to the database.

## Q10 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q52

A trigger is a stored procedure that the database management system fires automatically whenever a specified modification, an insert, update, or delete, occurs on a table, without any explicit user invocation. It has nothing to do with starting the DBMS, manual debugging, or user-login validation.

| 103 | Clipper | green |

## Q11 - Options
(A) π sid (σ age &gt; 20 Sailors) − π sid ((σ color = red Boats) ⋈ Reserves ⋈ Sailors)
(B) π sid ((σ color ≠ red ∧ age &gt; 20 (Boats ⋈ Sailors ⋈ Reserves)))
(C) π sid (σ age &gt; 20 Sailors) − π sid ((σ color = red Boats) ⋈ Reserves ⋈ Sailors)
(D) π sid (σ age &gt; 20 Sailors) ∧ π sid ((σ color ≠ red Boats) ⋈ Reserves ⋈ Sailors)

## Q11 - Hint
**Answer:** A, C
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q91

The correct strategy is set difference: start from every sailor with age over 20, then subtract out every sailor who has reserved at least one red boat, regardless of age.

π sid (σ age &gt; 20 Sailors) gives the sids of sailors older than 20.<br>
π sid ((σ color = red Boats) ⋈ Reserves ⋈ Sailors) gives the sids of sailors who reserved a red boat.

Subtracting the second set from the first gives exactly the sailors over 20 who have not reserved a red boat.

Options 1 and 3 are printed as byte-identical text in the source PDF itself, confirmed directly against the page image, and both show this correct expression. The color-comparison approaches in options 2 and 4 are unsound, since a sailor who has reserved both a red boat and a non-red boat would still wrongly satisfy a per-row color ≠ red condition on some other reservation.

## Q14 - Options
(A) ρ (Tempsids, (π bid Reserves) / π bid Boats) π sname ((Tempsids) ⋈ Sailors)
(B) ρ (Tempsids, (π sid,bid Reserves) / π bid Boats) π sname ((Tempsids) ⋈ Sailors)
(C) ρ (Tempsids, (π sid Sailors) / π bid Boats) π sname ((Tempsids) ⋈ Sailors)
(D) ρ (Tempsids, (π sid Reserves) / π bid Boats) π sname ((Tempsids) ⋈ Boats)

## Q14 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q94

Relational division needs a dividend that pairs the sid and bid attributes together, so the dividend must come from Reserves and include both columns.

- **A. ρ (Tempsids, (π bid Reserves) / π bid Boats) π sname ((Tempsids) ⋈ Sailors)** — wrong. The dividend keeps only the bid column, so dividing it by Boats bid column cannot produce any sid values.
- **B. ρ (Tempsids, (π sid,bid Reserves) / π bid Boats) π sname ((Tempsids) ⋈ Sailors)** — correct. Dividing the sid-bid pairs from Reserves by every bid in Boats yields exactly the sids that appear with all boats, and joining with Sailors retrieves their names.
- **C. ρ (Tempsids, (π sid Sailors) / π bid Boats) π sname ((Tempsids) ⋈ Sailors)** — wrong. The dividend is drawn from Sailors instead of Reserves, so it divides the wrong relation and cannot capture which boats a sailor reserved.
- **D. ρ (Tempsids, (π sid Reserves) / π bid Boats) π sname ((Tempsids) ⋈ Boats)** — wrong. The dividend keeps only sid with no bid to divide against, and the final join is with Boats instead of Sailors, so sname could not even be retrieved.

Only option B pairs sid with bid in the dividend and joins the result with Sailors, so it correctly computes sailors who reserved all boats.

## Q15
Which of the following relational algebra query computes the names of sailors who have reserved a red and a green boat?

Consider the relational schema of Sailors S, Reserves R, and Boats B given below.

**Table 1: Sailors S**

| Sid | Sname | Rating | Age |
|---|---|---|---|
| 22 | Dustin | 7 | 45.0 |
| 29 | Brutus | 1 | 33.0 |
| 31 | Lubber | 8 | 55.5 |
| 32 | Andy | 8 | 25.5 |
| 58 | Rusty | 10 | 35.0 |
| 64 | Horatio | 7 | 35.0 |
| 71 | Zorba | 10 | 16.0 |
| 74 | Horatio | 9 | 35.0 |
| 85 | Art | 3 | 25.5 |
| 95 | Bob | 3 | 63.5 |

**Table 2: Reserves R**

| Sid | Bid | Day |
|---|---|---|
| 22 | 101 | 10/10/98 |
| 22 | 102 | 10/10/98 |
| 22 | 103 | 10/8/98 |
| 22 | 104 | 10/7/98 |
| 31 | 102 | 11/10/98 |
| 31 | 103 | 11/6/98 |
| 31 | 104 | 11/12/98 |
| 64 | 101 | 9/5/98 |
| 64 | 102 | 9/8/98 |
| 74 | 103 | 9/8/98 |

**Table 3: Boats B**

| Bid | Bname | Color |
|---|---|---|
| 101 | Interlake | blue |
| 102 | Interlake | red |
| 103 | Clipper | green |
| 104 | Marine | red |

## Q15 - Options
(A) ρ (Tempred, π sid ((σ color = 'red' Boats) ⋈ Reserves)), ρ (Tempgreen, π sid ((σ color = 'green' Boats) ⋈ Reserves)), π sname (Tempred ∩ Tempgreen) ⋈ Sailors
(B) ρ (Tempboats 2, (σ color = 'red' Boats) ∩ (σ color = 'green' Boats)) π sname (Tempboats 2 ⋈ Reserves)
(C) π sname ((σ color = 'red' Boats) ∩ (σ color = 'green' Boats) (Tempboats 2 ⋈ Sailors ⋈ Reserves))
(D) ρ (Tempboats 2, (σ color = 'red' ∧ color = 'green' Boats)) π sname (Tempboats 2 ⋈ Sailors)

## Q15 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q95

The correct approach separately computes which sailors reserved a red boat and which reserved a green boat, and only then intersects the two sets of sailor ids.

Tempred holds the sids of sailors who reserved a red boat, and Tempgreen holds the sids of sailors who reserved a green boat. Intersecting them gives exactly the sailors who did both, and joining with Sailors retrieves their names.

The other options intersect the Boats relation directly on color, but no single boat row can be both red and green at once, so intersecting (σ color = 'red' Boats) with (σ color = 'green' Boats), or selecting color = 'red' AND color = 'green' on Boats, always produces an empty relation. Those approaches can never return a sailor.

## Q16
Statement I: A relational database schema represents the logical design of the database.<br>
Statement II: The current snapshot of a relation only provides the degree of the relation.

In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

## Q16 - Options
(A) Statement I is TRUE but Statement II is FALSE
(B) Statement I is FALSE but Statement II is TRUE
(C) Both Statement I and Statement II are FALSE
(D) Both Statement I and Statement II are TRUE

## Q16 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2021 (26 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q62

The schema (tables, attributes, constraints) is the logical design (Statement I true). A snapshot/instance of a relation shows both its degree (number of attributes) and its cardinality (number of tuples), not the degree alone, so Statement II is false.

## Q17
Given STUDENT(Rollno, Name, courseno) and COURSE(courseno, coursename, capacity), with coursename unique. Which of the queries below find the total number of students enrolled in each course together with its coursename?

```
-- Query A
SELECT coursename, count(*) 'total' FROM STUDENT NATURAL JOIN COURSE GROUP BY coursename;

-- Query B
SELECT C.coursename, count(*) 'total' FROM STUDENT S, COURSE C WHERE S.courseno = C.courseno GROUP BY coursename;

-- Query C
SELECT coursename, count(*) 'total' FROM COURSE C WHERE courseno IN (SELECT courseno FROM STUDENT);
```

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

## Q17 - Options
(A) A and B only
(B) C only
(C) A only
(D) B only

## Q17 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2021 (26 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q64

A and B both join STUDENT with COURSE on courseno and group by coursename, so count(\*) gives the enrolment per course. C never joins with STUDENT - it only filters courses that have at least one student and counts COURSE rows, so it cannot report the number of students per course.

## Q18
STUDENT and COURSE each have 3 attributes; COURSE has 3 records and STUDENT has 5 records. The relational-algebra query R = STUDENT x COURSE is executed. Match List-I with List-II for R.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. Degree of table R | I. 15 |
| B. Cardinality of table R | II. NIL |
| C. Foreign key of relation STUDENT | III. 6 |
| D. Foreign key of relation COURSE | IV. Courseno |

## Q18 - Options
(A) A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II
(B) A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II
(C) A-I, B-IV, C-III, D-II
(D) A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV

## Q18 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** SQL, Keys & Relational Algebra/Calculus
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2021 (26 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q65

The Cartesian product has degree 3 + 3 = 6 (III) and cardinality 3 x 5 = 15 (I). In the schema STUDENT.courseno refers to COURSE, so its foreign key is Courseno (IV); COURSE references no other table, so it has no foreign key - NIL (II).
